source.title: Improved state mixing in higher-order and block diagonal linear recurrent networks
source.authors: I. Dubinin; Antonio Orvieto; Felix Effenberger

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares language-model perplexity across recurrent architectures and block sizes at matched parameter counts, conceptually testing whether architecture shape has little effect. It does not fit or assess the power-law scaling relationships in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports language-model perplexity comparisons in Fig. 4, but does not report fitted power laws, extrapolations from small runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Results on synthetic tasks and cited scaling-law findings are outside the claim versions tested here.
record.test_reason: An architecture-design paper on linear recurrent networks. It cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation. Its language-model runs (140M–210M parameters, FineWeb) compare perplexity across block sizes of a recurrent state-transition matrix. That variable is an inductive-bias choice, not the depth/width/shape hyperparameters V4 concerns. The comparison is reported only in Fig. 4 with no numbers, so it cannot show whether differences are 'slight'. No power-law fit, extrapolation, compute-optimal split, downstream-versus-scale relation or fitting comparison is reported.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that state-mixing structure, rather than width alone, drives expressivity in linear RNNs, and that moderate block sizes work best. This rests mainly on synthetic tasks; small language-model runs (140M–210M) are said to show the same pattern. The authors note that large-scale language modeling is left for future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains and evaluates higher-order and block-diagonal recurrent architectures on language modeling; it does not reproduce the scaling-law measurement or fitting procedure of the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Perplexity outcomes vary with block size; the text also reports early saturation for diagonal models as hidden size increases.

fits_no_version.finding: At about 210M parameters and 10B tokens, BD-LRU with block sizes 2–8 reaches lower perplexity than the diagonal variant and block size 16 underperforms. Diagonal models saturate earlier as hidden size grows (140M–210M). All of this is shown in figures only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The recurrence structure (state-mixing block size) of linear RNN language models changes perplexity, and how perplexity scales with width, at matched parameter count.

record.problems: The language-modeling comparisons are shown in figures; numerical perplexity values and uncertainty estimates are not given in the text provided. The study does not fit power laws or test extrapolation.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute; the parameter range is under one order of magnitude.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
Depth, width and head shape of a fixed architecture are not varied at matched parameters; the block-size comparison is unquantified and concerns a different variable.
No other modality or training regime is examined for power-law form.
No downstream tasks are related to scale or loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 limits_scope verdict has been removed. The rows contain no values, and block size of a recurrent transition matrix is not the shape variable V4 refers to. Treat this study as off-topic for scaling laws.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit for held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute is reported.
No predictions from smaller runs are compared with much larger runs.
No fixed-compute search for an optimal parameter/token allocation is reported.
The study compares block sizes and model widths, but does not separately vary depth or test a broad range of other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No modality or training regime beyond text pretraining is evaluated for power-law form.
No downstream-task performance is related to scale or pretraining loss.
The study does not compare scaling-law fitting methods, fitted exponents, or compute-optimal splits across setups.
